title: GoMG: A Grammar of More Graphics!
description: GoMG: A Grammar of More Graphics! Abstract:Intricate scientific figures, mathematical diagrams, and infographics make complex information easier to reason about and more engaging. But it’s still difficult to make them. The Grammar of Graphics (GoG), which underlies most modern visualization software, eases this process for statistical charts by decomposing them into marks like bars, lines, and areas; and channels like shape, color, and size. While effective for statistical charts, this model does not directly support more bespoke visualizations that convey information through graphical structure like clustering and arrows. In response, researchers have built a slew of new grammars and GoG extensions, but these are difficult to engineer, mutually incompatible, and rarely make it out of the lab. Whether a more universal grammar of graphics can be built remains an open question.In this thesis, I present GoMG, a Grammar of More Graphics, which shows that the GoG, a diagramming language, and specialized grammars for unit, tree, and pictorial visualizations can be unified through a small set of core abstractions. Drawing on ideas from programming languages and compilers, I achieve this by combining the recursive composition of UI components with new formalisms for marks, channels, and graphical structure. I have released GoMG as an open-source Python and TypeScript library called GoFish that is designed to serve both as a practical tool for creating visualizations and a common substrate for future visualization systems research.Supervisor: Arvind Satyanarayan TBD July 30, 2026 Learning Interpretable and Reliable Classifiers Using Local Algorithms Jane Lange MIT Part Of Thesis Defense 2:00 P - 3:00 P Location 32-D463

title: Learning Interpretable and Reliable Classifiers Using Local Algorithms
description: Learning Interpretable and Reliable Classifiers Using Local Algorithms Abstract:       The safe and responsible deployment of machine learning in real-world applications requires learned models to satisfy critical safety, reliability, and interpretability constraints without compromising predictive accuracy or computational efficiency. This work addresses the challenge of enforcing three such critical properties: properness, adversarial robustness, and discrete Lipschitz continuity. Expressing these properties as global constraints to be enforcedthroughout the entirety of the training makes the problem computationally expensive.       To overcome this, we propose a framework based on “local correctors”—efficient query-time procedures that transform a base hypothesis satisfying a relaxed constraint into one that fully and strictly satisfies the target property. This localized approach reduces the complex globally-constrained optimization task during training to a relaxed version, which can then be solved efficiently using traditional polynomial approximation methods and standard optimization techniques. We design and analyze several such local correction algorithms and build learners and testers around them, producing provably safe and interpretable learned models with efficiency comparable to that of traditional learning.Thesis Committee: Mohsen Ghaffari, Ankur Moitra, Ronitt Rubinfeld, Li-Yang Tan TBD August 5, 2026 Accelerating Number-Theoretic Cryptography Using Vectorization and the Residue Number System Simon Langowski CSAIL 3:00 P - 4:15 P Location 32-G882

title: Instance-optimal estimation of L2-norm
description: Instance-optimal estimation of L2-norm Abstract: The $L_2$-norm, or collision norm, is a core entity in the analysis of distributions and probabilistic algorithms. Batu and Canonne (FOCS 2017) presented an extensive analysis of algorithmic aspects of the $L_2$-norm and its connection to uniformity testing. However, when it comes to estimating the $L_2$-norm itself, their algorithm is not always optimal compared to the instance-specific second-moment bounds, $O(1/(\varepsilon\|\mu\|_2) + t_\mu/\varepsilon^2)$, for $t_\mu = \|\mu\|_3^3 / \|\mu\|_2^4 - 1$, as stated by Batu (WoLA 2025, open problem session).In this paper, we present an unbiased $L_2$-estimation algorithm whose sample complexity matches the instance-specific second-moment analysis. Additionally, we show that $\Omega(1/(\varepsilon \|\mu\|_2) + t_\mu / \varepsilon^2)$ is indeed the per-instance lower bound for estimating the norm of a distribution $\mu$ by sampling (even for non-unbiased estimators).
